opus-5.5.text:
I think real-robot data is irreplaceable, but its role is often misunderstood. People sometimes frame it as a competition: real data versus simulation versus internet video, as if one source will win. I don't see it that way. Each source teaches the model something different, and real-robot data teaches the thing the others can't, which is how the physical world actually responds when *this* body touches it.

Internet video and language give you a broad prior. The model learns what a kitchen looks like, what "fold the towel" means, roughly how humans move their hands. Simulation gives you scale and the ability to try dangerous or rare situations cheaply. But both of them have a gap at the point of contact. Friction, deformable objects, cables, cloth, a slightly sticky drawer. The details of contact dynamics are where simulators are least faithful and where videos carry no action labels. That's exactly where real-robot data earns its cost.

So my view is that real-robot data should be spent where the gap is largest. You don't need millions of real trajectories teaching the robot what a cup is. You need real data that covers the long tail of physical interaction and recovery behaviors. A lot of the most valuable data is the messy kind: the grasp that slips and gets corrected, the object that's not where it was supposed to be. If you only collect clean, scripted demonstrations, the policy looks great in the lab and falls apart the first time something goes slightly wrong.

The second point is diversity over volume. Early on, many of us thought scaling meant more hours in the same few setups. What actually helps generalization is variety: different homes, lighting, objects, operators, and, increasingly, different robot embodiments. A thousand hours in one lab can be worth less than a hundred hours spread across fifty real environments. The agent has to learn what's invariant about a task, and it can only do that if it has seen the task under many different surface conditions.

Third, I think the most important real-robot data eventually won't come from teleoperation. Teleop is how we bootstrap, but it's expensive and it caps you at human demonstration quality. The long-term picture is a flywheel: you deploy a reasonably capable policy, it does useful work, and the data from that deployment, including its failures and the interventions, flows back into training. At that point the robot is collecting its own curriculum in the distribution it actually operates in. That's how you close the gap between benchmark performance and real-world reliability.

So in short: the broad prior comes from internet-scale data, scale and safety come from simulation, and grounding comes from real-robot data. The art is in using real data efficiently, targeting contact-rich, diverse, failure-inclusive experience, and building systems where deployment itself becomes the data engine.

r001.rationale: The response says internet data and simulation provide useful prior knowledge and scale, but does not state that any tasks can be performed very well without real-robot data.

r002.rationale: It calls real-robot data “irreplaceable” and explains that it provides physical grounding needed for contact-rich interactions and real-world reliability across varied settings.

fable-5.1.text:
Real-robot data is essential, but I think people often misunderstand what it's essential for. It's not that you need millions of real trajectories to teach a robot what a cup is or how a kitchen is laid out. Vision-language models already carry an enormous amount of that semantic and commonsense knowledge from the internet. What real data gives you is the part the internet fundamentally cannot: the physics of contact, the actual latency and noise of your sensors, the way a gripper slips on a wet surface, the way a drawer sticks. That gap between "I know what to do" and "my body can actually do it" is where real-world data earns its place.

So I think of it as a hierarchy. At the top you have web-scale pretraining, which gives you generalization in understanding. In the middle you have simulation, which is cheap and lets you cover long tails and dangerous situations, but always carries a sim-to-real gap. And at the bottom, closest to deployment, you have real-robot data, which is expensive and slow but is the only thing that tells the truth about your particular hardware in your particular environment.

The mistake I see is treating real data as something you collect once in a lab and then hope generalizes. In my experience, generalization across settings comes from diversity far more than from volume. A thousand episodes across fifty homes with different lighting, different objects, different operators will beat fifty thousand episodes in one lab cell almost every time. Diversity is what forces the model to learn the invariants rather than memorizing the scene.

And the other piece is that data collection shouldn't end at deployment. The most valuable real data is the data the robot generates once it's actually out doing tasks, especially the failures. If you can close that loop, so the system gets better the more it's used, then real-robot data stops being a one-time cost and becomes the compounding advantage. That, to me, is the real role it plays: not as the foundation, but as the thing that grounds everything else and keeps improving it.

r001.rationale: The response says web-scale models provide semantic and commonsense knowledge, but it does not clearly state that some tasks can be performed very well without real-robot data.

r002.rationale: The response calls real-robot data essential and says it is the only source of truth about particular hardware and environments. It does not clearly claim it is irreplaceable for strong performance across every real-world task and setting.

astra-6.text:
I think real-robot data is essential, but the key is what that data teaches the agent. A robot has to connect what it sees to what it does, and then understand the consequences. Contact, friction, an object slipping out of the gripper—those interactions are difficult to learn from observation alone.

For an agent to work across tasks and settings, diversity matters a lot. If you collect many demonstrations in one room with the same objects, you can get very good performance there without learning something that transfers. You want variation in environments, objects, starting conditions, and especially failures and recovery. The robot needs to learn what to do when its first attempt doesn't work.

I would see real-robot data as part of a broader learning system. Other sources can help build representations and teach useful priors, while real interaction grounds those capabilities in physical consequences. The important question is then: what additional experience would actually improve the robot? Collecting data around its weaknesses, testing in unfamiliar settings, and feeding those results back into training seems much more valuable than simply accumulating more hours.

r001.rationale: The response says demonstrations in one room can produce strong performance there, but does not say this can happen without real-robot data.

r002.rationale: It calls real-robot data essential and useful for grounding physical consequences, but does not state that it is currently irreplaceable across every real-world task and setting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think real-robot data is essential, but the key is what kind of generalization you expect it to support. A robot can succeed repeatedly on one task in one setup and still struggle when you change the object, the lighting, or the position of the camera. So collecting more repetitions alone doesn’t necessarily give you an agent that works broadly. You need diversity across tasks, environments, objects, and interactions.

Real-world interaction also exposes things that are difficult to learn from observation alone: contact, friction, how much force to apply, and what to do when an action doesn’t produce the expected result. Failed attempts and recovery can be especially useful, because deployment rarely looks like a perfect demonstration.

I would see real-robot data as part of a larger learning system. Other sources of data can help build representations and prior knowledge, while robot experience grounds those capabilities in actions and their consequences. The important question is whether each round of experience makes the agent more capable in settings it hasn’t already seen.

r001.rationale: It says repeated success on a task may not generalize, but does not state that tasks can be performed very well without real-robot data.

r002.rationale: It calls real-robot data essential and describes its grounding role, but does not say it is currently irreplaceable for performance across every real-world task and setting.
